Read this page Search for this page in the documentation of the latest stable release (version 2.5). C API Deprecations¶ Background¶ The API exposed by NumPy for third-party extensions has grown over years of releases, and has allowed programmers to directly access NumPy functionality from C. This API can be best described as “organic”. It has emerged from multiple competing desires and from multiple points of view over the years, strongly influenced by the desire to make it easy for users to move to NumPy from Numeric and Numarray. The core API originated with Numeric in 1995 and there are patterns such as the heavy use of macros written to mimic Python’s C-API as well as account for compiler technology of the late 90’s. There is also only a small group of volunteers who have had very little time to spend on improving this API. There is an ongoing effort to improve the API. It is important in this effort to ensure that code that compiles for NumPy 1.X continues to compile for NumPy 1.X. At the same time, certain API’s will be marked as deprecated so that future-looking code can avoid these API’s and follow better practices. Another important role played by deprecation markings in the C API is to move towards hiding internal details of the NumPy implementation. For those needing direct, easy, access to the data of ndarrays, this will not remove this ability. Rather, there are many potential performance optimizations which require changing the implementation details, and NumPy developers have been unable to try them because of the high value of preserving ABI compatibility. By deprecating this direct access, we will in the future be able to improve NumPy’s performance in ways we cannot presently. Deprecation Mechanism NPY_NO_DEPRECATED_API¶ In C, there is no equivalent to the deprecation warnings that Python supports. (gh-32835) New functions# New function numpy.top_k# A new function np.top_k(array, k, axis=..., mode=..., sorted=...) was added, which returns the largest/smallest k values of an array along a given axis. (gh-31659) Abstract DType classes# The numpy.dtypes namespace now exposes new abstract DType classes: NumberAbstractDType, IntegerAbstractDType, SignedIntegerAbstractDType, UnsignedIntegerAbstractDType, InexactAbstractDType, FloatingAbstractDType, and ComplexFloatingAbstractDType. These support checks such as isinstance(arr.dtype, np.dtypes.NumberAbstractDType) and can be passed as the kind argument to numpy.isdtype. They are also exposed through the C API, for example for promotion rules (some of these previously already existed in C). Custom DTypes can opt in by inheriting from the appropriate abstract class. (gh-31755) New function numpy.minmax# A new function np.minmax(a, axis=..., out=..., keepdims=..., initial=..., where=...) was added, which returns a (min, max) tuple holding the minimum and the maximum of an array along a given axis. It is equivalent to (np.min(a, ...), np.max(a, ...)) but computes both in a single fused pass over the data. For dtypes that support min/max but have no fused minmax loop (such as the string DType and other user DTypes), it falls back to two separate reductions. A masked-array counterpart np.ma.minmax was also added, which simply returns (np.ma.min(a, ...), np.ma.max(a, ...)). (gh-32231) Deprecations# numpy.linalg.lapack_lite is deprecated# Importing numpy.linalg.lapack_lite is deprecated. The module is an internal implementation detail of numpy.linalg and was never intended as a public API. Users that need LAPACK or BLAS routines should use scipy.linalg.lapack or scipy.linalg.blas instead. (gh-32015) Future Changes# Python scalar promotion in append will change# In a future NumPy verison, numpy.append will follow the scalar promotion rules of numpy.concatenate. For example, appending 1 to a uint8 array will leave the dtype of the result uint8. Appending 300 will raise OverflowError. Operations that will result in a different dtype or a warning in the future now generate a FutureWarning.
